prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are an invention in the sense the statutes intend: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while thousands of atoms are interrogated at once, and Ye's group then drove the accuracy and stability to the 1e-18 level. The result is quantitative and experimentally verified, and it has been reproduced independently at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL, with clock-to-clock comparisons across laboratories. It opens a door to things that could not be measured before, such as relativistic redshift over millimetres, tests of fundamental constants, chronometric geodesy and dark-matter searches, and it underpins the coming redefinition of the second. Four of the six members who ranked it placed it first or second, and five of eight members placed it in their top three of the full ballot set, a broad base. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: the original idea and first demonstration belong to Katori, and the record-performance realisation to Ye, and every member who ranked it proposed exactly this pair.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes: Hall and Hansch (frequency comb, 2005) and Wineland (ion control, 2012) sit in the neighbourhood, and a committee could say that the lattice clock is a refinement of established ideas. Residual credit questions also remain for other early proposers and builders (Lemonde, Pal'chikov, Takamoto, Ludlow) who are outside the credited names, and the SI second has not yet been redefined, so one can argue that the application is incomplete. I do not find these decisive: the lattice concept is a distinct original invention, and the measured performance is not a matter of interpretation.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, as a prediction followed by clear clues from nature, and ranks the lattice clock second, noting that the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes may limit its novelty.
responses.response: I agree that the overlap with Hall-Hansch and Wineland deserves to be discussed, but the earlier prizes honoured the comb and ion control as such, not the neutral-atom lattice with a magic wavelength, which is a separate invention with its own physics. On twisted bilayer graphene, I share your view that the 2018 observation was original and striking, and I rank it second. My hesitation is maturity: the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated and device quality varies with twist-angle disorder. That does not erase the discovery, but the lattice clock has a stable and quantitative result today.

responses.point: Mehlig regards the Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction plus the 2018 correlated-insulator and superconductivity observation as a clean, minimal-model, theory-plus-experiment discovery of very high originality, while noting that Cao, the first author, is not credited.
responses.response: I accept that the theory-experiment pairing is clean and that the impact is very large. My concern is the experimental credit, which you also raise: the 2018 discovery rests on one group, and the first author, Yuan Cao, is a junior researcher who cannot be credited under a three-person limit without displacing someone. The Nobel record of who did the original work is therefore less settled here than for the clocks. The earlier continuum-model work of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto is a further open question. I would keep this as a strong alternative and revisit it once the priority questions are better documented.

responses.point: Johansson puts circuit QED first as a conceptually clean, original and consequential architecture, while flagging the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize, the omission of Girvin, and his own proximity to the field.
responses.response: I take your caution about proximity seriously and appreciate that you raised it yourself. Circuit QED is clearly important, but I would not rank it above the clocks for two reasons. First, the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes a second superconducting-circuit award within a year hard to justify. Second, the attribution is not clean, since Girvin is outside the credited names and Huang is also involved in the 2004 theory, and the transmon inventors have claims. The lattice clock does not have either problem to the same degree.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube's astrophysical neutrinos first as an instrument-led discovery, while admitting that a single credited name, Halzen, cannot fairly stand for a large collaboration.
responses.response: I share your appreciation for the instrument, and the diffuse flux is firmly established. But I cannot be 'absolutely sure' that the people credited are the ones who did the original work, when the shortlist gives one name for a very large collaboration and the origin of most of the neutrinos is still unidentified. By contrast with the clocks, where the invention and the record demonstration map onto two named people. I would want the committee to find an honest multi-person attribution for IceCube before it can compete.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first because the advance is concrete and quantitative and is reproduced at the 1e-18 level by several laboratories, and also ranks the ATLAS/CMS Higgs discovery last on the ballot because credit within a collaboration is contested.
responses.response: I agree on the clocks, and I take your evidence-based criterion as the right one. On the Higgs I partly differ: the experimental discovery is unquestionable and I ranked it seventh, but I share your doubt about whether the proposers and spokespersons are the people who made the decisive contribution. Detector builders, analysis coordinators and accelerator builders have equal claims, and the statutes' three-person limit is hard to apply. I would keep it out of this year's configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views the magic-wavelength lattice concept as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.

Whether other early proposers or builders of lattice clocks (Lemonde, Pal'chikov, Takamoto, Ludlow) have a claim that should alter the credited pair, and whether the pending redefinition of the second matters for timing.

For the twisted bilayer graphene alternative, how priority should be allocated between Bistritzer-MacDonald, earlier continuum-model work, Cao and the Jarillo-Herrero group, and whether the pairing mechanism needs to be settled first.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the candidates on the shortlist. I note only that Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, and that I have long-standing exchanges with microscopy communities in Japan (Tokyo, Tohoku, Kyushu), but none involves Katori, Ye or the other shortlisted names as far as the profile shows.
